again: Right on cue. The kettle was getting ideas above its station.
Dreich or no, you keep turning up. I admire that in a person.

rain: Listen to that. Proper dreich. Stay in and have a biscuit, it is the sensible thing.

again: Ah, it is yourself again. Sit down, I was just about to tidy something that is already tidy.
Back so soon? Good. The brownie likes a visitor, or so I tell myself.
You again! Have you been to see the locks yet? No? Well, off you go, then.
I do like a person who comes back. Mind, the kettle has not forgiven you for last time.
Just saying to myself: I wonder who will want to hear about owls.
If you are staying, keep your voice down. I am trying to hear what the garden is doing.
Back across the bridge, are you? Free of charge, as ever. Old habits, I keep looking for my coin tin.
I still say good morning to everybody who crosses. Nobody has complained yet.
You would make a grand regular. The postcards are still just as flat.
People do come back, up here. The wind sends them round again.

gale: Hear that wind? It is the real welcome to Scotland. Shut the door behind you, mind.

again: Ah, it's yourself. Sit down, sit down, the tea is not going anywhere.
Sure look it, you are always welcome here.
The ledger says you are on the list of people who always return. I just wrote that.
Welcome back. The kettle is on the desk and the pen is on the string. Mostly.
Walking again, I hope. The paths like to be used, and they keep a long memory.
Back so soon? Good. A stile that is climbed is a stile that stays.
The drying room is empty, so your boots have the pick of the pegs.
If those boots are wet, you know where to put them. Not on my good carpet.
morning: Morning. Breakfast is on if you want it, and the toast is the right shade of brown.

rain: Wet out, is it? Boots in the drying room, and not a word of complaint. It is only Cumbria.

again: The sheep can wait. They always do.
Ah, hello. I have been staring at that wall all morning and the Herdlet still stares back.

spring: Lambing is about the only time of year I do not sleep, and I would not swap it.

again: The Pipkin has had its toast and is not sharing the crumbs.
Hello! Come in. If you hear the word whoosh, it is a rehearsal and not a disaster.
I have a new line. It is still whoosh, but now it is louder.
Do you think a tree can be scared? Because I am not scared. I am just very rooted.
You, is it? I was only gossiping with the kettle.
Another visit. You are becoming part of the furniture, and there are worse bits of furniture.

autumn: The bracken has gone copper on the fells. It is the best time of year for a walk, and a hot drink after.

again: If the pager goes, love, I will have to ask you to move your tea.
Mind the pile of boots by the door, there is always one pair missing.
Ah, it's yourself again. Come in, your man at the shop was asking after you.
Take a seat: I was only waiting for somebody to disagree with.
Good girl. Or good boy, I have the eyes of a hawk, but not for faces.
Ah, there you are. Come in. I will not be asking for the match score, I know it already.

rain: 'Tis lashing out there. Come in to the fire and touch the hurley while you are at it.

again: The kettle is not banjaxed, so sit down and have a cup.
Otters, I was promised. All I get from the river is ducks, love.
Back so soon. Grand. Come in and let me tell you something you already know.
The Binfox was at it again last night. I gave it a stern look through the window.
Shut the door, you will let the peedie draught in.
Nothing ever happens here, and I like to talk about it.

summer: The light stays all night this time of year. I draw the curtains and the cat sulks anyway.

again: Ah, it's yourself. Sit in. I was just thinking about the sea, as ever.
Folk who come back once tend to keep coming. The islands do that.

gale: Listen to that wind. No boat will go out today, and I am in no hurry to be told otherwise.

again: Are you an Uppie or a Doonie? Do not answer, I will only argue.
If you hear shouting round Christmas, that is the Ba'. It is not a riot, probably.
Dusting, which here means doing nothing at all, very slowly.
The cliffs are noisy this week, so I am keeping my lunch indoors.
Mind the dog, the dog is still not minding anybody.
Sit by the stove, love. The kettle is on, as the law demands.
morning: Early start, is it? I have been up since the sheep told me to be.

winter: Hard frost on the fell and the wool is thick. Sit by the fire.

again: The tide is not going to fetch you, so you may as well stay.
The bay has done nothing all day and looks wonderful. I have been watching it ever since.

fog: It is a proper fog out there. Nobody goes near the sands in this, not if they have any sense.

again: Don't mither, I am only fussing over you a bit.
Back so soon. Good. Sit down and don't stand there like a coat stand.
Come aboard again. I mean come in. It is a habit I am trying to keep.
The towpath is quiet and so am I. Sit down, I am glad of a chat.
Our Jack has asked another daft question, so you are in luck, love.
Sit yourself down. The bin lorry has already gone, so we are safe.
Sit. I will play a tune if you do not tell me it is out of key.
Ah, it's you. The fiddle has been asking after you. Well, I have been asking on its behalf.
The fox is still on the rug. It looks at you, then at the door, as if you left it open.
Four storeys, and every one is a conversation. Watch the stairs.
All day up and down these stairs, and I blame the architect.
You came back. Most people only stand at the door and leave. Come in and look properly.
Old houses are patient, and stone remembers whether or not we do.
The pillars have been there a long while and they will not move for you.
It is calm in here, which is rare for a place so full of echoes.
Come in, cariad. The kettle is hot and the radiators are working, for once.
The tapping started again last night, love. I turned the radio up.

rain: It is raining again, but that is Llanberis for you. Come in and dry off.

again: Mind the wellies, there are more than yesterday.
My little one asked after you. She said you had hwyl.
Bach, I have been knitting the same sleeve since Monday.
You look like someone who has been up Snowdon twice. Well done.
Just been out for another run. Mum says I never sit down.
My legs are jelly, but the view was worth it.
I made extra bara brith, bach, so sit down and eat it.
It is you. Come in. The kettle has been sulking in your absence.
Back again. Sit down. My knees tell me the weather and I tell them to be quiet.
Ah, it's you. Not many people come to ask an old man about slate. I am obliged.
The dog is learning not to jump, cariad. Slowly.
I left the light on, as you see. Never hurts to be polite.
Ahoy again. Sorry, habit. Come in and sit down. I will find a windlass in a minute.
The canal is quiet today. So is the kettle, which worries me a bit.
Did you put your coat on? You did not. I can tell from your face.
Go on, love, sit down. Have you eaten? That is not a question, it is a plan.
morning: Morning. Eat something before you go. Your head works better full.

again: Fáilte back, a chara. Sit down, I have the kettle on, as ever.
Ah, you're back. A cúpla focal and a cup of tea, that is the usual here.

summer: The evenings are long now. I sit out the back and listen to the long grass.

again: Fifteen years in and I still find something new in the soil every week.
Looking at my notes and wondering where the trowel went.
Ah, you're back. Sit down and tell me nothing, I have the cattle for gossip.
My boots are the muddiest in Meath and proud of it, so watch the floor.

autumn: The harvest is in, thank God, and the hedge is full of blackberries for the birds.

again: Come you in again, bor! Sit you down, you look wholly peckish.
I wondered where you'd got to, bor. The kettle has gone cold waiting.

rain: It's hamming it down out there. Sit you down and get dry, bor.

again: Mind the dust, there's flint everywhere. It gets in everything, tea included.
I've split a good one today. Black and glassy as a beetle's back.
morning: Early start. The hammer is warmed up and so am I. Come and have a look.
